questions.q: What is the key difference between a plan from EXPLAIN PLAN / DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY and one from DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR?
options: EXPLAIN PLAN predicts a plan without running the SQL; DISPLAY_CURSOR shows the plan actually used by a statement that already executed
They always show identical information
DISPLAY_CURSOR only works on SQL Server, not Oracle
EXPLAIN PLAN is only available in Oracle 19c and later
questions.explain: EXPLAIN PLAN is a prediction; DISPLAY_CURSOR reflects the plan Oracle genuinely executed, which is more trustworthy, especially with actual row counts via gather_plan_statistics.

questions.q: In a DBMS_XPLAN tree, which line generally executes first?
options: The most-indented line inside a group
Always the very first line printed, top to bottom
The line with the lowest Id number, regardless of indentation
Whichever line has the highest cost
questions.explain: Plan output is indented to show parent/child relationships, and the most-indented (innermost) operation within a group typically runs first, feeding its parent.

questions.q: Is TABLE ACCESS FULL always a sign of a performance problem?
options: No — for a small table or a query needing most of its rows, a full scan can outperform an index
Yes, it should never appear in a healthy plan
Only Oracle 21c eliminated TABLE ACCESS FULL entirely
It only ever appears due to a missing statistics job
questions.explain: TABLE ACCESS FULL is a normal, sometimes optimal choice; it's a red flag mainly when it appears against a large table for a highly selective predicate.

questions.q: What does the Predicate Information section beneath a plan show?
options: Which predicates drove access (narrowing what's read) versus filter (discarding rows after reading) at each numbered plan step
The exact wall-clock time each operation took
A list of all indexes that exist on the table, used or not
The SQL text of the original statement only
questions.explain: Predicate Information distinguishes access predicates, which narrow what's actually read, from filter predicates, which discard rows after they've already been retrieved.

questions.q: When is a NESTED LOOPS join typically efficient?
options: When the outer (driving) input is small and the inner input has a good index to probe
Only when both inputs are extremely large with no indexes
Only for full table scans on both sides
Nested loops are never efficient in Oracle and should always be avoided
questions.explain: Nested loops probe the inner input once per row of the outer input, so they shine when the outer input is small and the inner probe is cheap via an index.
